name: Spotify Mix
title: What if your playlist knew how to DJ?
tagline: Helping listeners understand — and trust — Spotify's mixing recommendations.

heroMedia.alt: The redesigned Spotify Mix edit-transition screen in motion

meta.value: Mobile app, inside Spotify's design system

meta.label: Methods
meta.value: Quant survey · moderated testing · confidence scoring

intro: Spotify Mix lets listeners craft smooth transitions between songs — matching keys, aligning BPM, choosing blend curves. Powerful, and built on knowledge most listeners simply don't have.
I redesigned the experience so that understanding arrives in context, at the moment you need it — designed inside Spotify's existing system, not around it.

sections.label: The problem
sections.heading: Smooth transitions required knowledge most listeners didn't have
body: Mixing well means understanding BPM compatibility, key matching, and what makes a transition sound intentional. In my survey, most respondents reported little or no familiarity with mixing terminology — and 9 of 11 who tried to learn the feature still felt confused afterward.

In moderated testing the pattern sharpened: multiple participants didn't realize Spotify even had a Smart Reorder feature moments after confidently reviewing the full interface, and participants repeatedly hunted for explanations whenever an unfamiliar concept appeared.

sections.label: The opportunity
sections.heading: Make mixing approachable without dumbing it down
body: The redesign focused on reducing the cognitive load of mixing: simplifying decisions, providing guidance when users needed it, and keeping the full editing power in place for people who wanted it.
Two moments carried most of the confusion — editing a transition, and understanding what the system had already done for you. Those became the redesign's spine.

sections.label: Foundation
sections.heading: Simplifying transition editing
body: Many participants reported limited familiarity with mixing terminology, and primarily used presets when creating transitions. The redesigned editing experience keeps the dual-waveform view but promotes presets to the primary path, labels actions in plain language, and tucks advanced controls behind a deliberate step — accessible, not ambient.

items.alt: Redesigned edit-transition screen: dual waveform, blend curves, presets, plain-language actions
'Making mixing easy' onboarding sheet: match key color and keep BPM close

media.caption: The core edit screen, and the onboarding sheet that frames the two rules that matter: match the key color, keep BPM close.

sections.label: Foundation
sections.heading: Bringing Smart Reorder forward
body: Smart Reorder — Spotify reordering your playlist for better transitions — was the feature participants loved most and found last. During testing, people simply couldn't find it, and once they did, the system's reasoning was invisible.
The redesign surfaces it as a first-class action and explains what changed and why, so the automation builds trust instead of suspicion.

items.alt: Smart Reorder confirmation showing what will change and why

media.caption: Smart Reorder, surfaced — with its reasoning made visible before you commit.

sections.label: Education
sections.heading: Tap to learn more — teaching inside the moment
body: Simplifying alone doesn't build understanding. Wherever a concept like BPM or key compatibility appears, it's tappable: a short contextual explanation opens right where the question occurred, then gets out of the way.
In testing, participants successfully applied BPM and key concepts after receiving these contextual explanations — knowledge that a settings-buried help page had failed to transfer.

items.alt: Learning in context — tapping an unfamiliar term opens a short inline explanation

media.caption: Concepts explain themselves where they appear — not in a help center.

sections.label: Problems to solutions
sections.heading: Fixing a rough transition, step by step
body: The hardest task in testing was recovering from a transition that sounded bad. One participant put it plainly: "This is not as helpful… I have to try to figure it out on my own."

The redesign flags the hard blend directly on the timeline and offers a labeled fix — including adding a bridge song when two tracks simply don't want to meet. Directly labeled actions replaced guesswork.

items.alt: A hard blend flagged and highlighted on the transition timeline
The add-a-bridge-song flow suggesting a track to smooth the transition

media.caption: The rough-transition story: the problem is pointed at, and the fix is one labeled action away.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.heading: Design for different levels of involvement
body: Across usability testing, participants consistently rated the redesign higher than Spotify's current experience for confidence and understanding — average confidence moved from 2.6 to 3.7 out of 5, and every participant preferred the redesign.

The deeper lesson: some users wanted quick answers, others wanted detailed control. The redesign works because it serves both from the same screens — high-level clarity by default, depth one deliberate tap away.
